newsitem.title: UK: Polish city of Gdansk targets foreigners with bond.
newsitem.headline: Polish city of Gdansk targets foreigners with bond.

text.p: Better known as the birthplace of Poland's Solidarity trade union movement and for its troubled shipyard, the City of Gdansk aims to make its name on international capital markets with an inaugural bond issue.
The city will debut with the first tranche of a 99.3 million zloty ($35 million) municipal bond on December 16, the first domestic currency issue from the region aimed at foreign funds.

"We need the money to stop the degradation of our infrastructure which has occured over the past 40 years and has had a disastrous effect on our city," the Mayor of Gdansk Tomasz Posadki told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.
The first tranche of 11.5 million zlotys, of which 3.9 million is aimed at overseas investors, will be issued on December 16 in a four year bond priced at 105 basis points over Polish treasuries.
It will be secured on the assets of the city.
The ground-breaking deal for Gdansk comes as cities in central and eastern Europe are searching for capital outside the tight purse strings of cash-strapped central governments.
Russian, Czech and Romanian cities have announced they will make issues, although they are planning dollar eurobonds for overseas investors rather than local currency issues.

"Every city in eastern Europe will eventually have to look at this route. Central government cannot afford to carry all of the responsibility," said Pascal Najadi, a vice president of Merill Lynch, which is managing the international issue.
Najadi said that a eurobond would have been too large for Gdansk's spending needs and would have generated foreign currency risk that the city did not need.
Gdansk, which celebrates its millenium next year will use the proceeds of the bond to build a road link with its airport and ring rad and develop public transport.
"Our streets are becoming clogged as car ownership in Poland has increased and it is essential to have a better infrastructure in place to attract more foreign investment," the mayor said.
He said that Gdansk, which has attracted around 13 percent of the foreign direct investment in Poland since 1990, would in future spend a quarter of its budget on infrastructure projects.
Posadki said that at present the city budget was in surplus and he expects revenues to continue rising as Poland's economy, which is growing at seven percent a year, accelerates.
"Gdansk has mainly been known for Solidarity and the shipyard, now we want to create an image that Gdansk is a place for foreigners to invest," the mayor added.

He said that land from the Gdansk shipyard, which is in eceivership, would eventually be used to construct a new civic centre and an industrial park, leaving the yard at one third of its current size.
Even with redundancies from the yard's 7,000 strong workforce, Posadki is optimistic on the future for the local economy.
"We must change, but with unemployment at just five percent in the region, employers have difficulty finding skilled people," the mayor said.
